prompt:
Write an opinion piece of about 500 words on whether software teams should stop estimating how long work will take. Take a side and argue for it. The readers are working engineers and their managers.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
Software teams should stop estimating how long individual pieces of work will take. I mean the habit of asking each engineer for a number of days or points, adding the numbers up and presenting the total as a date. I do not mean that teams should stop planning, and I do not mean that managers should stop asking when something will be ready.

The first reason is that the numbers are poor. In Thinking, Fast and Slow, Daniel Kahneman describes a team he worked with that was writing a school curriculum. Each member guessed the book would take between a year and a half and two and a half years. A colleague who knew how similar projects had gone said that about two in five never finished, and that those which did finish took between seven and ten years. The team took eight. The Sydney Opera House was budgeted at 7 million Australian dollars and opened ten years late at about 102 million. Most software is smaller than either, but the cause is the same. People estimate the work they can picture and leave out the work they cannot, and in software that is most of it.

The second reason is the cost. An estimation meeting takes several people for an hour or more, and its output is treated as a commitment even when everyone in the room knows it is a guess. Engineers learn to pad the figure. Managers learn to cut the padding. The number that results has little to do with the work and a good deal to do with the negotiation.

The third reason is that a better source of prediction already exists. A team's record of finished work says more than its opinion of unfinished work. Suppose a team has merged between eight and fourteen pull requests a week for the last quarter, and the backlog for a release holds sixty items of roughly similar size. The range of finishing dates can be read straight from those figures. Sixty items at fourteen a week is a little over four weeks, and at eight a week it is seven and a half. Nobody has to guess, and the forecast changes when throughput or scope changes. To do this the team has to cut work into pieces of about the same size, which is a useful habit whether or not anyone forecasts anything.

Some will say that the business needs dates for contracts, for launches and for coordination with other departments. That is true, and it is the reason to prefer a range drawn from past output over a single date built from individual guesses. A manager can plan around a range of four to eight weeks, provided they are told that it is a range. When the date is fixed in advance, the useful question is how much will fit, and watching throughput answers it better than a sum of estimates made months earlier.

Teams that make this change will notice that they have dropped a ritual. In my view they will not miss it. What was useful in estimating was the conversation that exposed what nobody had understood about the task, and that conversation can still happen when the team splits the work, with no number attached at the end of it. The number was the part that was wrong.
